samples.summary: Another account's archived document content is never collected by any sweep, so an expired session leaves full documents on a shared device indefinitely
samples.evidence:
`collectStale` sweeps live entries across all users (deliberately, per the comment at line 1005: "a shared device's other account is precisely the one that never comes back to run its own housekeeping"), but the archive sweep at line 1037 passes `this.userId` as `onlyUser`, so `dropArchivesWhere` skips every archive row belonging to anyone else. Cross-checking every other caller of `dropArchivesWhere`: `dropAllForUser` (line 985) uses `IDBKeyRange.only(userId)` and is only ever invoked with the signed-in or the pending-erase identity, and `dropArchivesForDocument` filters on `BY_USER` = `this.userId`. There is no path that collects a departed account's archives.

The attack/exposure chain: user A opts in on a shared machine and edits. Their session cookie expires — which `api/auth.ts:255-266` itself calls "the commonest way a session ends" — so `fetchWithAuth`'s 401 arm calls `logout({ eraseLocalData: 'keep-archives' })`, and `eraseOfflineDataOnLogout` (offline-erase.ts:165-169) deliberately spares the archives AND, on that branch, does not clear `rememberOfflineUser`. A never returns to that machine. Their archives — whole gzip'd CRDT snapshots plus change logs, i.e. document text — now sit in the origin's IndexedDB forever: user B's session sweeps A's *live* entries at 30 days but provably cannot touch A's archives, A's own sweep never runs, and `dropAllForUser` is never called with A's id again. Anyone with the browser profile (the next user of the shared workstation, devtools, forensic imaging) reads them directly.

This is the exact population the design's own § Storage cleanup table names the 30-day sweep as the backstop for, with archives carved out of it and no replacement backstop supplied.

samples.summary: Offline-copy recovery is offered even when the revocation reconcile failed, letting an archive from a revoked workspace be materialized into a new server-side document
samples.evidence:
The three housekeeping steps in `OfflineRuntime` each have their own `try/catch` (lines 103-119 for the reconcile, 123-132 for the recovery offer), so a failed `fetchDocuments()` is swallowed at line 118 and execution falls straight through to `offerRecoverableWork` at line 127. The suite pins this behaviour: `offline-runtime.test.tsx` "keeps sweeping when the reconcile fails" rejects `fetchDocuments` and then asserts `toastWarning` was called.

`purgeRevokedOfflineDocuments` is, by the design's own § Storage table, the ONLY mechanism that removes content after somebody else revokes access — every other purge runs on the device of whoever made the request. So the chain is: user A is removed from workspace X while offline or while the listing endpoint is failing; A's device still holds an archive for a document in X; the reconcile that would have dropped it (`purgeOfflineDocuments` with `archives: 'drop'`) throws and is logged; the recovery toast is still shown, and clicking "Save a copy" runs `recoverOfflineCopy`, which calls `createDocument` and `applyImportedContent` to push that content back to the server as a new document A owns and can then re-share.

That converts locally-held bytes into a fresh, durable, shareable server-side artifact derived from content A is no longer authorized to read. Ordering the recovery offer after a *successful* reconcile (or skipping it when the listing failed) closes it. Confidence is medium because `recoverOfflineCopy` currently fails at the `createDocument` call for an unrelated reason (see the separate workspace-scoping finding), so the last step of the chain is blocked today rather than by design.

samples.summary: The explicit erase ("turning this off deletes them" / sign-out) walks the header index, so a snapshot row whose header is missing survives it
samples.evidence:
`dropAllForUser` enumerates keys with `headerKeysWhere(BY_USER, IDBKeyRange.only(userId))` at line 948 and purges only those. A snapshot row with no header beside it is therefore unreachable by the erase that backs both the Settings toggle's "turning it off deletes what was stored" and the sign-out erase.

The only path that reaches such a row is `collectStale`'s `orphanSnapshotKeys()` (line 1095), and that filter excludes `belongsToAnotherUser(docKey)` — so the owner's own orphan is collectable only if the owner returns to the device and waits out a sweep, and another account's orphan is never collectable by anyone else at all. The row still holds the gzip'd document snapshot, which `inflate` recovers verbatim.

The store's own comment at line 1043 states the hazard exactly ("a permanent quota leak holding document content that logout cannot erase") and then fixes it only in the collection path, not in the erase path. The orphan shape is rare — `atomically` was added specifically to prevent a torn `saveSnapshot` from producing one — which is why this is minor rather than major, but the erase is a user-facing promise about content and it has a reachable gap.

samples.summary: Offline-copy recovery creates the new document with no workspace, so the copy's placement is not derived from the archived document's origin
samples.evidence:
`recoverOfflineCopy` calls `createDocument({ title, type: source.type })` at line 210 (and `{ title, type: 'note' }` at line 196). The frontend `createDocument` payload type (`api/documents.ts:11-17`) has no `workspaceId` field, and it POSTs to `/documents`, whose handler (`packages/backend/src/document/document.controller.ts:197-224`) begins `await this.workspaceService.assertMember(body.workspaceId, userId)` and then `workspace: { connect: { id: body.workspaceId } }`.

Nothing in the recovery path consults `describeArchivedDocument`'s result, the archive's `docKey`, or any record of which workspace the archived document belonged to — the archive record (`ArchiveRecord`) stores `docKey` and `userId` but no workspace. So the destination is whatever the backend resolves from an absent `workspaceId`. Today that fails closed: `resolveId(undefined)` stringifies to `"undefined"`, fails the UUID regex, misses the slug lookup and throws `NotFoundException`, so recovery 404s rather than misfiling. But the *invariant* — a recovered copy must land in a workspace the user is still entitled to, ideally the archive's own — is nowhere enforced in the client, so any backend change that gives `POST /documents` a default workspace would silently materialize content from workspace X into that default, where its members can read it.

Severity is minor because it fails closed against the current backend; the missing scoping is the finding.
searchedFor: grep createDocument across packages/frontend/src — only api/documents.ts defines it; offline-copy-recovery.ts:196,210 are the recovery call sites
read api/documents.ts:11-30 — payload type has title/type/fileId/fileSize/mimeType, no workspaceId
grep @Post('documents') in packages/backend/src/document/document.controller.ts — assertMember(body.workspaceId, userId) then workspace.connect
read offline-copy-recovery.ts — no workspaceId, no reference to the archive's origin workspace
read wafflebase-doc-store.ts ArchiveRecord — stores docKey, snapshot, meta, changes, archivedAt, userId; no workspace

samples.summary: The path-traversal regression test was relaxed from "every request URL carries the id encoded" to "some request URL does"
samples.evidence:
The pre-change loop asserted both properties per URL: `expect(pathname).not.toContain('/auth/logout')` AND `expect(pathname).toContain(encodeURIComponent(TRAVERSAL))`. The change keeps the first as a universal over `paths` but demotes the second to a single `paths.some(...)` at lines 166-170, to accommodate `deleteWorkspace`'s new companion `fetchDocuments()` call that carries no id.

The core traversal guard is intact — the `/auth/logout` normalization check still runs on every URL, so a raw `../../auth/logout` id in any request pathname is still caught. What is lost is the encoding invariant: a future companion request that places the id somewhere the WHATWG normalizer does not collapse into the pathname (a query string, a fragment, a header built from the same id) would now satisfy `some` via the *other* request and never be checked itself. Note the surviving assertion inspects `new URL(raw, ...).pathname` only, so a query-string carrier is outside it entirely.

This is a reduction in coverage of an injection guard rather than a live vulnerability — I traced no current call site that puts an id in a query string on these routes — but it is exactly the kind of weakening that makes the next unsafe call site land silently, and no lane will flag it since the suite stays green.

verdict.reason: Every factual claim in the finding checks out against the tree. wafflebase-doc-store.ts:1037-1041 passes `this.userId` as `onlyUser`, and dropArchivesWhere:1165-1178 skips any archive id not in the signed-in user's BY_USER key set, so the 30-day sweep provably cannot touch another account's archives even though its live-entry half at :1023-1032 is deliberately cross-user. I enumerated every other archive-deleting caller: dropAllForUser:985 (IDBKeyRange.only(userId)), dropArchivesForDocument:858-870 and listArchives:885-896 (BY_USER = this.userId) — none is unscoped. The exposure chain is reachable: auth.ts:250-267 invokes logout with eraseLocalData 'keep-archives' on a failed-refresh 401, auth.ts:125-127 maps it to keepArchives:true, and offline-erase.ts:165-169 takes the branch that clears only the pending-erase marker while leaving rememberOfflineUser intact, so retryPendingOfflineErase:191-213 has nothing owed and offline-runtime.tsx:57 then overwrites the identity with the next account. purgeRevokedOfflineDocuments (:271-278), purgeOfflineDocuments (:230-234) and watchForOfflineDisable (:328-346) all scope to the current offlineUserId and cannot reach the departed account's rows. The design doc confirms the carve-out rather than a backstop: offline-local-persistence.md:279-280 says archives stay scoped, while :466 and :512 claim archives are subject to the same 30-day collection. A deliberate tradeoff documented in prose is not a guard; full document content (gzip'd snapshot plus inlined change log, ArchiveRecord at :86-95) belonging to an account whose session ended persists indefinitely in the shared device's IndexedDB, which is sensitive-data-exposure within this lens. No named refutation ground applies.

finding.summary: Offline-copy recovery is offered even when the revocation reconcile failed, letting an archive from a revoked workspace be materialized into a new server-side document
finding.evidence:
The three housekeeping steps in `OfflineRuntime` each have their own `try/catch` (lines 103-119 for the reconcile, 123-132 for the recovery offer), so a failed `fetchDocuments()` is swallowed at line 118 and execution falls straight through to `offerRecoverableWork` at line 127. The suite pins this behaviour: `offline-runtime.test.tsx` "keeps sweeping when the reconcile fails" rejects `fetchDocuments` and then asserts `toastWarning` was called.

`purgeRevokedOfflineDocuments` is, by the design's own § Storage table, the ONLY mechanism that removes content after somebody else revokes access — every other purge runs on the device of whoever made the request. So the chain is: user A is removed from workspace X while offline or while the listing endpoint is failing; A's device still holds an archive for a document in X; the reconcile that would have dropped it (`purgeOfflineDocuments` with `archives: 'drop'`) throws and is logged; the recovery toast is still shown, and clicking "Save a copy" runs `recoverOfflineCopy`, which calls `createDocument` and `applyImportedContent` to push that content back to the server as a new document A owns and can then re-share.

That converts locally-held bytes into a fresh, durable, shareable server-side artifact derived from content A is no longer authorized to read. Ordering the recovery offer after a *successful* reconcile (or skipping it when the listing failed) closes it. Confidence is medium because `recoverOfflineCopy` currently fails at the `createDocument` call for an unrelated reason (see the separate workspace-scoping finding), so the last step of the chain is blocked today rather than by design.

verdict.reason: The code is exactly as described — offline-runtime.tsx:103-119 swallows a failed `fetchDocuments()` and falls through to `offerRecoverableWork` at :127, and offline-runtime.test.tsx:146-152 pins that behaviour — so this is not `not-present`. It is refuted as out-of-scope for the Security lens. (1) No authorization decision is bypassed: `createDocument` (api/documents.ts:11-30) POSTs only `{title,type}` with no workspace or source-document identifier, so `recoverOfflineCopy` (offline-copy-recovery.ts:210-213) creates a brand-new document owned by the caller in their own workspace — no cross-tenant write, no IDOR, no gate stepped around. The server-side ACL on the original document in the revoked workspace is untouched. (2) The content is already disclosed to the actor: the archive is the former member's own local IndexedDB copy of a document they were authorized to read while a member; re-uploading bytes you already possess into your own account crosses no confidentiality boundary, since the same actor can exfiltrate them by any other means. (3) `purgeRevokedOfflineDocuments` is opportunistic hygiene, not an enforcement path — offline-erase.ts:288-290 swallows all of its own internal errors and returns 0, and the sweep runs once per session, so a device that stays offline or never opens the app is never purged either. Client-side remote-wipe is structurally unenforceable and is not a security control. (4) The suggested remediation does not close the chain: the toast at offline-runtime.tsx:184-229 is rendered once at session start with `duration: Infinity` and is never re-validated, so a revocation landing after a *successful* reconcile leaves the same clickable "Save a copy" action — confirming this is an ordering nicety rather than a gate. None of the lane items (authz gates, secrets, injection, crypto/signature verification, SSRF, deserialization, traversal) apply; at most this is a `minor` data-retention hardening suggestion, which is not blocking under this rubric. It may be a valid correctness/design observation for another lens.

finding.summary: The thirty-day sweep is scoped to the signed-in user, so a departed user's document content is never collected and persists indefinitely on a shared device
finding.evidence:
`collectStale()` builds `mine` from `headerKeysWhere(BY_USER, IDBKeyRange.only(this.userId))` (line 893-895) and then skips every aged key with `if (!mine.has(docKey)) continue;` (line 903). `dropArchivesWhere(BY_ARCHIVED_AT, range, this.userId)` (line 915-919) is scoped the same way, and `orphanSnapshotKeys()` skips other users via `belongsToAnotherUser` (line 982). The only caller is `OfflineRuntime`, which constructs the store with `userId = String(me.id)` of whoever is signed in (offline-runtime.tsx:55-62, PrivateRoute.tsx:35).

Attack/exposure chain: user A enables offline saving on a shared or borrowed machine and edits documents; A's session later ends without a deliberate "Log out" (see the 401 finding below), or A simply never returns. User B then signs in. Every sweep from then on runs with `this.userId = B`, so A's snapshots, change logs and archives — full gzip'd document content — are filtered out of the candidate set on line 903 and are never deleted. There is no origin-wide or unattributed-row cleanup: `dropAllForUser`, `purgeDocument`, `purge` and `evictOldest` are all user-scoped too. The content stays on disk until the browser profile is wiped. Every other cleanup path in this change explicitly names this sweep as its backstop (`workspaces.ts:92` "a failure leaves the thirty-day sweep to it", `offline-erase.ts:115`, `documents.ts:163`), so those paths' residual risk is unbounded rather than thirty days.

verdict.reason: The finding's mechanism is not in the code. `collectStale()` (wafflebase-doc-store.ts:999-1053) sweeps `headerKeysWhere(BY_UPDATED_AT, range)` at line 1023 with NO user scoping, and purges every aged, non-live entry at 1030-1032 regardless of who wrote it — the opposite of the claim. There is no `mine` set and no `if (!mine.has(docKey)) continue;` anywhere in `collectStale`; the `mine` set the reviewer quotes is in `evictOldest` (1262-1271), an unrelated method where scoping is deliberate. The cited line numbers 893-919 land in `listArchives`/`loadArchive`, not the sweep. `headerKeysWhere` (1133-1143) takes only `(index, range)` and has no userId parameter, so the quoted call cannot compile. The code comment at 1005-1018 states the cross-user policy explicitly, and cleanup.test.ts:187-218 pins it ("collects another account's stale entries but never their archives", asserting `theirs.load("theirs-old")` is undefined after user-1's sweep). The only residual scoping is archives (1037-1041) and header-less orphans (1104, 1121-1124); archives are a documented exception because they are the sole copy of unreconciled work, and they are unreadable across accounts — `listArchives` (889) and `loadArchive` (913) both reject rows whose `userId` differs — so no cross-user content exposure exists. The claimed chain (user B signs in, A's snapshots and change logs are filtered out and persist forever) is false for the live content stores.

finding.summary: Access revoked by another user (workspace member removal) never purges the removed member's locally persisted copies; the comment asserting a cleanup that does not exist makes the gap read as covered
finding.evidence:
`removeMember` gates the purge on `isOfflineUser(String(userId))` (line 137), which is correct for the caller's own device — but the comment on line 130-131 claims "The removed member's own device cleans up when they next open the app." No such code exists. `OfflineRuntime` (components/offline-runtime.tsx:74-97) runs exactly two things on mount: `store.collectStale()` and `offerRecoverableWork()`. Neither consults the server for what the user may still read; there is no reconciliation of stored `docKey`s against `fetchDocuments()` or any permission endpoint.

Concretely: an owner removes collaborator B from a workspace (or from wafflebase entirely) from the owner's browser. B's device holds full, decompressible copies — snapshot plus change log — of every document in that workspace B had opened with offline saving on. Nothing on B's device deletes them. The only backstop is `collectStale`, which is thirty days at best and, per the finding above, never runs at all if B does not sign in on that device again. The same hole applies to any server-side downgrade of B's role to viewer, or removal of B from a single document, since no client-side purge is wired to those either.

The design document states the rule this violates outright: "content must not outlive the authority to read it" (docs/design/offline-local-persistence.md, § Storage cleanup table: "Document deleted, or workspace access lost | Drop that entry").

verdict.reason: The finding claims no client-side reconciliation exists on the removed member's device and that the comment in api/workspaces.ts asserts a cleanup that does not exist. Both are false. `purgeRevokedOfflineDocuments` (packages/frontend/src/lib/offline-erase.ts:268-294) diffs `store.storedDocumentIds()` against the server-provided accessible set and purges everything outside it, dropping archives too — explicitly for the revoked-access case. It is wired into the OfflineRuntime mount effect at packages/frontend/src/components/offline-runtime.tsx:103-119, which awaits `fetchDocuments()` and passes the ids in (imported at line 13, documented in the component's trigger table at line 34, and covered by tests at offline-runtime.test.tsx:132 and 143). The comment at api/workspaces.ts:149-153 names that exact function, so it describes present, reachable code rather than a phantom cleanup. The reviewer's stated reading of offline-runtime.tsx ("exactly two things on mount") does not match the file.

finding.summary: Session expiry (401) deliberately skips the offline erase and leaves the recorded identity in localStorage, so the commonest way a session ends on a shared machine leaves full document content on disk
finding.evidence:
The 401 arm of `fetchWithAuth` calls `logout({ ..., eraseLocalData: false })` (line 258), so `eraseOfflineDataOnLogout()` is not invoked (line 121-123) and `rememberOfflineUser(undefined)` — which is only reached from inside that function (offline-erase.ts:119) — never runs. Two consequences on a shared or public machine:

1. The user's snapshots, change logs and archives stay in IndexedDB. The reasoning in the comment (they will "log straight back in on the same device") holds for the author's own laptop and not for the shared-workstation case the whole feature is justified by — and a user who closes the tab and walks away never issues a deliberate `logout()` at all, so `eraseLocalData: true` is only reached by someone who clicks "Log out".
2. `wafflebase-offline-user` (offline-erase.ts:53) is left in localStorage holding the departed user's id, a persistent identifier of who last used the machine, readable by the next visitor and by any same-origin script.

Combined with the user-scoped `collectStale` finding, the retention here is not bounded by thirty days: if the next person to sign in is somebody else, the sweep filters the departed user's rows out permanently.

verdict.reason: The finding's central factual claim is not present in the code. (1) There is no `eraseLocalData: false` — the option type is "all" | "keep-archives" (auth.ts:20-35) and the 401 arm passes "keep-archives" (auth.ts:266). (2) `eraseOfflineDataOnLogout(...)` is NOT skipped: logout() calls it unconditionally at auth.ts:125-127 on every path, including the 401 arm, before the response check and before the redirect. The reviewer's cited "lines 121-123" are comment text, not a conditional. (3) `keepArchives` does not preserve document content wholesale: wafflebase-doc-store.ts:948-971 purges every live header/entry for the user regardless of the flag, and the flag only skips `dropArchivesWhere` at wafflebase-doc-store.ts:984-986. So a 401 expiry does erase snapshots and change logs from IndexedDB; only the SDK-unreconciled archives (the only copy of work the server never took) deliberately survive. The one accurate sub-claim — that `wafflebase-offline-user` stays in localStorage on the keepArchives branch (offline-erase.ts:165-169) — is a deliberately retained opaque user id, not a credential, token or key, kept so a later deliberate sign-out or the recovery UI can name the account owning the surviving archives; it is readable only by same-origin script, which already has access to the IndexedDB content itself. That is hardening at most and does not sustain a major security finding once the "full document content left on disk" premise is refuted.

finding.summary: `eraseOfflineDataOnLogout` forgets the identity before the erase has succeeded and swallows the failure, so a transient IndexedDB error at logout permanently strands document content with no retry path
finding.evidence:
`const who = offlineUserId(); rememberOfflineUser(undefined); if (!who) return;` (lines 118-120) clears both the module state and the `wafflebase-offline-user` localStorage mirror *before* `eraseOfflineData(store, who)` is attempted, and the attempt's failure is caught and downgraded to `console.warn` (lines 124-130). `logout()` then shows `toast.success('Logged out successfully')` (api/auth.ts:129) and redirects.

So if `store.dropAllForUser(who)` rejects — the database is blocked by another tab's connection (`open()` rejects on `onblocked`, wafflebase-doc-store.ts:373-379), storage is momentarily unavailable, or a transaction aborts — the user is told the sign-out succeeded while their document content remains on the device, and the identity needed to retry is gone. A later `eraseOfflineDataOnLogout()` finds no `who` and returns immediately (line 120-122). Per the first finding, `collectStale` will also never reach those rows if a different account signs in next. Recording the identity only after a confirmed erase, or leaving it in place on failure, would keep the promise retryable.

verdict.reason: The quoted code does not exist in this repository. The finding claims eraseOfflineDataOnLogout clears the identity before attempting the erase and leaves no retry path. In offline-erase.ts:150-182 the order is inverted from what is claimed: `await eraseOfflineData(store, who, options)` runs first (line 160), and `rememberOfflineUser(undefined)` is only reached on the success path (line 171). The `rememberOfflineUser(undefined)` at line 155 sits inside the `if (!who)` early-return branch, where there is by definition no identity to strand. On failure the catch block does the opposite of the claim: it persists the owing identity via `rememberPendingErase(who)` (line 178) into the `wafflebase-offline-erase-pending` localStorage key (line 115). The retry path the finding says is missing exists as `retryPendingOfflineErase()` (lines 191-213) and is invoked unconditionally from the authenticated shell's mount effect at components/offline-runtime.tsx:84, before the new session writes anything — covering exactly the 'a different account signs in next' scenario the finding says is unreachable. The code comment at lines 162-164 explicitly records that the clear-first ordering was the previous behavior and was deliberately changed. The only surviving element of the finding — that the erase never throws and logout still reports success — is documented intentional behavior (lines 145-148) now backed by a durable retry marker, and is a correctness/UX tradeoff rather than an authorization, secret-exposure, injection, or crypto defect under the security rubric.

finding.summary: Archives are exempt from access-loss purging and the recovery path re-materializes the whole document, letting a user create a permanent copy of content they are no longer authorized to read
finding.evidence:
`purgeDocument` deliberately spares archives (lines 753-757: "Archives are deliberately left alone"), and `purgeOfflineDocuments` — the function `deleteDocument`, `deleteDocuments`, `deleteWorkspace` and `removeMember` all call — routes only through `purgeDocument` (offline-erase.ts:154). Meanwhile `document-purged` ("the document was deleted or GC'd upstream") is one of the three `LocalChangesDropped` paths that create an archive in the first place.

The archive is not a diff of the user's unsent edits: `remove()` stores `record.snapshot` — the entire serialized document — alongside the log (lines 697-708), and `rehydrateArchive` rebuilds the full root, which `readContent` then reads whole (offline-copy-recovery.ts:202, offline-copy.ts `rehydrateArchive`). `recoverOfflineCopy` passes that to `createDocument` + `applyImportedContent` (offline-copy-recovery.ts:210-212), producing a new document owned by the recovering user.

Chain: an owner deletes a shared document (or a collaborator is removed and the document is subsequently GC'd for them) → the collaborator's SDK emits `document-purged` → `remove()` archives the full document → on the collaborator's next sign-in `OfflineRuntime` shows "Save a copy" (offline-runtime.tsx:148-156) → clicking it creates a permanent document in the collaborator's own workspace containing the entire content, including the parts they did not author, after the owner revoked it. The archive is only dropped once that copy is written (line 212), so declining the offer keeps the content and re-offers it every session.

verdict.reason: The pivotal evidence is misdescribed and the access-loss paths are already guarded. `purgeDocument` (wafflebase-doc-store.ts:813-829) takes `archives?: "keep"|"drop"` and calls `dropArchivesForDocument` (858-874) on "drop"; the cited lines 753-757 are the archive `put` inside `remove()`, not a "deliberately left alone" decision in the purge. `purgeOfflineDocuments` (offline-erase.ts:226-246) forwards a `dropArchives` option, and both true access-revocation callers pass it: `deleteWorkspace` (workspaces.ts:136) and `removeMember` (workspaces.ts:167), each `{ dropArchives: true }`. The removed member's own device is reconciled by `purgeRevokedOfflineDocuments`, which purges everything the server no longer lists with `{ archives: "drop" }` (offline-erase.ts:285) and is invoked at offline-runtime.tsx:116 BEFORE `offerRecoverableWork` at offline-runtime.tsx:127, so a revoked document's archive is gone before "Save a copy" can be offered. What is left is the document-deletion path, which keeps the archive by documented design (802-811): the archive is written only under the `expectLoss` latch while the user was attached and authorized (711-770), its snapshot is frozen at that moment so it cannot hold post-revocation content, archives are userId-scoped on both read paths (885-896, 907-922) so no other principal gains access, and a deleted document is gone for everyone rather than revoked per-user. The residual gap I did find — `storedDocumentIds()` walks header keys only (843-855) while `remove()` deletes the header, so an archive predating a removal escapes the reconcile — concerns bytes the user lawfully possessed before revocation, making it retention hygiene rather than an authorization bypass or cross-principal exposure, i.e. below this lens's blocking bar.
